turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Oh, sorry we're late. The car park was an absolute shocker and she wouldn't undo her seatbelt.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): No worries, you're here. Come and sit. How old are you, love?
[SEG0003] person_3 (PATIENT): Five. Um. Are we in trouble for being late?
[SEG0004] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She's just turned five. Wound up all morning, sorry about that.

[SEG0005] person_4 (NURSE): Got the obs while you were coming through. Temp's thirty six point seven, pulse a hundred and eight, sats ninety eight percent, blood pressure ninety six over sixty two. Wriggly, but the numbers are decent.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thanks, all of that looks fine. Mia, what's been bothering you?
[SEG0007] person_3 (PATIENT): The car was hot. And I don't like those chairs.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): They are a bit scratchy, hey. Is it just the chairs, or is something else itchy?
[SEG0009] person_3 (PATIENT): My knees are itchy.
[SEG0010] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Yeah, that's why we're here. Itchy dry patches behind both knees and in the elbow creases. She's scratching them raw, worse at night, and it wakes her up.
[SEG0011] person_2 (DOCTOR): How long's this been going?
[SEG0012] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Six weeks. It faded for a couple of days, then came straight back.
[SEG0013] person_3 (PATIENT): It wakes me up. I scratch and scratch. Will I have to have a needle? Is that bad?
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): No needle today, promise, and it's a nuisance not an emergency. Mum, any weeping, or yellow crusts on the patches?
[SEG0015] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Mm, I suppose. Sometimes, not really. Mostly just dry and she picks at it.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): Alright, I won't call that an infection. Any cough, or trouble with her breathing?
[SEG0017] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No cough. Breathing's been fine, she was tearing around the park yesterday.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): Anyone at home with asthma, or eczema?
[SEG0019] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Her dad's had asthma since he was a kid. I get a bit of hay fever in spring, nothing else.
[SEG0020] person_3 (PATIENT): So will I get daddy's asthma? Is the itchy thing forever?
[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): Not automatically, sweetheart. They can run in families, but lots of kids only get the skin part. What creams have you been using?
[SEG0022] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): A big white tub a few times a day, and a little yellow tube at night that the chemist gave us. I can never remember the names, we just go by the colour.
[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): Do you know if the yellow one was a steroid?
[SEG0024] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Err, someone said hydrocortazone, the one percent one, but I wouldn't swear to it. Might be wrong.
[SEG0025] person_3 (PATIENT): The yellow one stings a bit. Do I have to keep using it? What if it stings worse?
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): We can stop anything that stings. Any allergies to creams or medicines?
[SEG0027] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No, nothing like that. She's never reacted to a medicine.
[SEG0028] person_4 (NURSE): She was picking at both elbows in the waiting room. I left the skin alone, didn't put anything on.
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good to know. Mia, can I have a look at your knees and elbows? I won't do anything that hurts.
[SEG0030] person_3 (PATIENT): Ok. But will it hurt? I don't want it to hurt.
[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): Just eyes, no poking. Skin behind both knees and both elbow creases is dry and a bit thickened, with scratch marks. No weeping, and it's not hot.
[SEG0032] person_3 (PATIENT): Do I look weird? Are they gonna laugh at me at kindy?
[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): You don't look weird at all. From those dry itchy patches in the creases, I'd call this eczema, atopic dermatitis. That's my working impression, not a final stamp.
[SEG0034] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Ok. So do we chuck the yellow tube? And is the white tub even doing anything? Google's been no help.

[SEG0035] person_2 (DOCTOR): Stop the yellow tube, and stop the white tub too, we don't know what's in it. I'll prescribe methylprednisolone aceponate ointment, zero point one percent, that's Advantan, a thin layer once a day on the patches only, for two weeks. And QV cream, the plain moisturiser, at least three times a day, plus straight after a bath. Steroid first, give it a minute, then the QV.
[SEG0036] person_3 (PATIENT): Three times? That's heaps. Will the new cream sting me?
[SEG0037] person_2 (DOCTOR): The ointment's usually kinder on cracked skin than a cream is. Thin smear only. If a patch gets redder, or hot, or starts weeping, stop and ring the clinic.
[SEG0038] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Baths though? A mum at playgroup reckons no soap and oats in the water. Is that actually right?

[SEG0039] person_2 (DOCTOR): Short lukewarm baths are fine. No soap on the sore patches, pat dry, moisturise straight away. Oats are optional, not the treatment, and please don't put the steroid on her face.
[SEG0040] person_3 (PATIENT): Can I still swim? What if the pool makes it bad?
[SEG0041] person_2 (DOCTOR): Swimming's fine. Rinse the chlorine off and put the moisturiser on after, or the skin will dry out.
[SEG0042] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Should we do a blood test, or those allergy pricks? Her cousin had the whole lot.
[SEG0043] person_2 (DOCTOR): Not today. If the patches aren't settling after the two weeks of ointment, we can look at allergy testing then. No pricks this visit.
[SEG0044] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): And follow up, do we come back only if it's worse?
[SEG0045] person_2 (DOCTOR): Come back in two weeks either way so I can check the skin. Reception will book it as you leave.
[SEG0046] person_4 (NURSE): I'll walk you out and get that two week review in the book. You were brave, Mia.
[SEG0047] person_3 (PATIENT): Ok. Bye. It still itches.

spec.situation: Mother brings a child with itchy dry patches behind the knees and elbows, worse at night, scratching; creams named by colour; father has asthma; doctor adjusts steroid cream and moisturiser advice.

traps.happens: The conversation OPENS with a remark, joke, apology for being late, small talk, or a trigger event (a relative's diagnosis, a neighbour's advice, the receptionist's note) BEFORE the real reason is stated. The patient states the real concern a few turns later.
traps.label_rule: chief_complaint is the real concern in a short phrase in the patient's wording (e.g. 'worried about diabetes', 'voice gets tired'). NOT the opening remark, the joke or the trigger (the relative's illness goes into family_history only if it is a relative's condition said as such).

features: ambiguous_answer: an answer that sounds like yes but is really 'maybe' ('mm, I suppose', 'sometimes, not really'); recorded with uncertainty or not at all, never as a firm fact.

spoken_numbers: doses, vitals and durations are spoken as words or sloppy speech ('a hundred and two point five', 'one-forty over ninety', 'five-ish years', 'twenty milligram'); the label writes them normally (102.5, 140/90, 20 mg) and does not turn vague ones into exact ones.

bad.reason: Patient reports yellow tube stings a bit; severity mild/body site implied, but current temporality not explicit.

omissions.text: Rash was reported to be worse at night and wakes her up; the itching specifically wakes the child from sleep.
The rash faded for a couple of days and then came straight back.
Possible weeping/yellow crusting was asked about; family said only 'sometimes, not really', mostly just dry and she picks at it, and the doctor concluded they would not call it infection.
No medication allergies or cream allergies, and specifically she has never reacted to a medicine.
Current yellow tube cream was possibly hydrocortisone 1%, but the family member was unsure of the name.
Doctor advised the ointment formulation is usually kinder on cracked skin than a cream.
Advantan instruction included applying a thin layer only to the patches only.
QV cream should be used straight after a bath in addition to at least three times a day.
Allergy testing/blood tests were explicitly deferred for this visit: 'Not today' and 'No pricks this visit.'
Follow-up was to occur in two weeks regardless of whether the skin is better or worse ('either way').
